title: SECURE 2.0 Automatic Enrollment Final Rule: Count Every Restaurant Location as One Employer, Test the 10-Employee and 3-Year Exemptions From Payroll, and Budget the 3 Percent Deferral Before the Next Plan Year

content:
The SECURE 2.0 automatic enrollment final rule, issued November 17, 2026, counts every commonly owned restaurant location as one employer when it tests the 10-employee exemption, so a group of LLCs with one 401(k) is usually covered. Here is how to run the headcount from payroll, book the 3 percent deferral, and budget the cash before the next plan year.

Why now: the final rule landed on November 17, 2026, and the statute has applied since 2025

On 2026-11-17 the IRS announced IR-2026-141, the final regulations under section 414A that implement the SECURE 2.0 automatic enrollment mandate for 401(k) and 403(b) plans. Covered plans must enroll eligible employees at an initial rate of 3 percent, raise the default by at least one percentage point a year until it reaches at least 10 percent, and stop no later than 15 percent. Employees can opt out or pick their own rate at any time. The Treasury release of the same day lists the exceptions: qualifying small and new businesses, governmental plans, church plans, and SIMPLE 401(k) plans.

Two dates matter, and they're easy to confuse. The regulations themselves apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2027. The statute, though, has applied to plan years beginning after December 31, 2024, and in between a plan has to follow a reasonable, good faith interpretation of section 414A. The technical analysis of Treasury Decision 10061 published on 2026-11-17 notes that following the January 2025 proposed regulations, Notice 2024-2, or the final regulations satisfies that standard. So a restaurant plan adopted in 2023 that has never defaulted anyone in isn't waiting for 2028. It may already have a correction to make.

Why this matters for restaurants in particular: the final rule settles how employees are counted for the 10-employee exemption, and it counts them across every entity under common ownership. Most multi-location groups run one LLC per store and one plan for the group. The per-store headcount that looks exempt isn't the number the rule uses.

Count every commonly owned location as one employer

Three questions decide whether a plan is covered, and all three are answered from documents you already have: the plan document, the entity formation records, and last year's payroll.

Is the plan grandfathered? A 401(k) whose cash or deferred arrangement terms were adopted before December 29, 2022 is outside section 414A. The final rule measures the date the plan terms were adopted, not the date deferrals began. A plan adopted in 2023 or later is in scope unless an exemption applies. Merging a newer plan into a pre-enactment plan keeps the exemption only if the older plan is designated as the ongoing plan in writing and the merger lands inside the section 410(b)(6)(C) transition period.

Is the employer new? The exemption for an employer that has been in existence for less than three years looks through to predecessors under the section 415 predecessor rules. Buying the assets of a restaurant that has operated for a decade generally means you inherit its age for this test. Check the formation date of the oldest entity in the group and any acquired predecessor.

Does the employer normally employ 10 or fewer? This is where multi-location groups get caught. The final rule adopts the COBRA counting method: an employer normally employs more than 10 employees if it had more than 10 on at least 50 percent of its typical business days during the preceding calendar year. Under that same COBRA rule, part-time employees count as a fraction of a full-time employee based on hours, so a store with six full-timers and a bench of part-timers is not a six-employee store. And the term employer includes every member of a group treated as a single employer under sections 414(b), (c), (m), or (o). Three LLCs with the same owners are one employer for this test.

Two more rules sharpen the headcount. Once an employer first exceeds 10, the exemption survives for the one-year period after the close of that taxable year and then ends, and it does not come back if headcount later drops below 10, including after a corporate event. In a multiple employer plan or pooled employer plan, the small and new business exceptions are applied employer by employer, so joining a PEP doesn't change the answer.

Here is the test for a three-location group with common ownership, using a 40-hour full-time week and last year's payroll. Each store's manager would tell you their location is small. The group is not.

Pull the census from payroll by entity and pay period for the preceding calendar year, convert part-time hours to full-time equivalents on the plan's full-time basis, and add the entities together. If the group count exceeds 10 on at least half of the days the restaurants were open, the small employer exemption is gone. If you already track hours by job code for the tip credit, the same time data feeds this count. The job-code time tracking that survived the 80/20 withdrawal is the same source.

What the 3 percent default does to payroll, the books, and cash

Auto-enrollment changes the cash timing of payroll and, if the plan has a match, the benefits expense. It doesn't change gross wages. Getting the entries right keeps the P&L honest and the balance sheet clean.

The default deferral is the employee's money. Each pay run, the deferral is withheld from net pay and sits in a liability until it is deposited with the recordkeeper: debit wages expense for the full gross as always, credit 401(k) deferrals payable for the withheld amount, and credit cash for the rest of net pay and the taxes. On deposit, debit the payable and credit cash. The Department of Labor's safe harbor for plans with fewer than 100 participants treats a deposit made within seven business days of the pay date as timely, so the payable should clear inside that window every cycle. A deferral booked to an expense account double counts wages and overstates labor cost.

The match is different, and it is optional. An eligible automatic contribution arrangement, which is what section 414A requires, carries no matching contribution requirement; only the plan's own terms do. If the plan matches, the match is an employer expense by location: debit benefits expense, credit employer contributions payable. That is the number that moves prime cost, and it belongs on the location P&L next to wages and payroll tax, not in a corporate overhead bucket.

Budget it in three lines. First, eligible headcount after the plan's age and service rules, including long-term part-time employees who become eligible after two consecutive years of at least 500 hours. Second, average plan compensation, which for most restaurant plans is W-2 wages and therefore includes reported tips. Third, the stay rate. Treasury's own economic analysis behind the final rule assumes participation rises about seven points, from roughly 70 to 77 percent, and that about half of covered employees stay at the default rate rather than choosing their own.

For the 30-employee group above, say 26 are eligible and average plan compensation is $2,600 a month including tips. The default deferral is $78 per person per month. If every eligible employee stayed enrolled at 3 percent, the group would withhold $2,028 a month and hold it briefly as a liability. If the plan matches dollar for dollar up to 3 percent, the match is up to $2,028 a month of new expense, about $24,300 a year, before opt-outs. At a 50 percent stay rate, halve both. Then step the default up a point a year: the match stops growing once the plan's match cap is reached, but the withheld liability keeps rising until the default reaches 10 percent.

Two restaurant-specific wrinkles. First, a tipped employee with a cash wage near the federal $2.13 floor can have a paycheck too small to cover 3 percent of total compensation plus taxes once tips are counted. Ask the payroll provider how it handles a deferral that exceeds available net pay, and document the answer, because how the plan treats that shortfall is a plan term, not a payroll setting. Second, the 90-day permissible withdrawal lets a newly enrolled employee take the default deferrals back. That refund comes from the plan, not the restaurant, and any match tied to it is forfeited under the plan's terms, so the only employer entry is the reversal of a match accrual that hasn't been deposited yet.

If the plan was adopted after December 29, 2022 and new hires were never defaulted in, that is a missed deferral failure. The self-correction window under Rev. Proc. 2026-34 is longer than it used to be, but the reduced corrective contribution still depends on catching the error fast, so run the headcount test before year-end rather than after.

Accounting controls for the auto-enrollment file

Keep the exemption file and the payroll tie-out as one package, with four layers separated so a reviewer can see what is fact, what is arithmetic, what is judgment, and who signed.

Source data. The plan document showing the adoption date of the deferral terms. The ownership chart for every entity and the formation date of each, including acquired predecessors. The payroll census for the preceding calendar year by entity and pay period, with hours. The recordkeeper's deposit confirmations. The opt-out and rate election forms with dates.

Deterministic calculation. Full-time equivalents by day from hours. The 50 percent of business days test on the aggregated count. The three-year anniversary of the oldest entity or predecessor. For each pay run, deferral equals plan compensation times the employee's rate, with the default applied to anyone who has no election on file. The escalation schedule by plan year, with the final rule's flexibility on timing and amount documented as a plan choice rather than left to payroll.

Reviewer checks. Tie the 401(k) deferrals payable to zero after each deposit and tie the deposit to the recordkeeper confirmation by pay date. Tie total deferrals withheld in the period to the recordkeeper's contribution report. Tie match expense by location to the match deposited. Confirm every employee who became eligible in the period either has a default deferral on the first eligible paycheck or a dated election. Confirm the payable and the match sit in the right entity, because a deferral withheld by one LLC and deposited by another is an intercompany balance that needs its own entry.

Decision owner. The plan sponsor, usually the owner or the management company, decides the exemption position, the default rate within the 3 to 10 percent band, and the escalation path, on advice from the third-party administrator or ERISA counsel. The controller runs the test and the tie-out and documents both. Payroll executes the rate. Nobody at store level changes a deferral rate without a signed election.

Polarity matters here. Deferrals payable and match payable are credits that should return to zero each deposit cycle; a persistent balance is either a late deposit or a booking error. The match is a flow that belongs in the period the wages were earned, not the period the deposit cleared. The headcount test is a point-in-time count taken day by day across the prior year, which is why pay-period averages are only an approximation and should be labeled as one in the file.

Limits and common mistakes

  • Testing each LLC alone. The rule aggregates entities under common ownership. A group of small stores is one employer, and the per-store count is not the test.
  • Reading 2028 as the start date. The regulations apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2027, but the statute has applied since plan years beginning after December 31, 2024. A covered plan that has never auto-enrolled is already behind.
  • Assuming the plan is grandfathered after a provider change. Amending a pre-2022 plan keeps its status. Adopting a new plan with a new provider usually does not, and a merger needs the ongoing-plan designation in writing.
  • Counting only full-time employees. Part-time employees count as fractions under the COBRA method. Servers and hosts on 20 hours a week add up.
  • Booking deferrals as expense. Deferrals are withheld wages and a liability. Only a match, if the plan has one, is expense.
  • Treating a slow season as a reset. Once the group exceeds 10, the requirement stays even if headcount later falls below it.

This is an accounting workflow, not legal advice. The plan document and the regulation control, and the exemption position should be confirmed with the plan's administrator or counsel before the next plan year begins.

Frequently asked questions

Does the SECURE 2.0 automatic enrollment rule apply to a restaurant group with three LLCs of eight employees each?

Usually yes, if the plan's deferral terms were adopted on or after December 29, 2022 and the group has existed for three years. The final rule counts all members of a group under common control as one employer, so three LLCs with eight employees each normally employ 24, well over the 10-employee exemption.

When do restaurants have to start automatically enrolling employees?

The statute has applied to plan years beginning after December 31, 2024 under a reasonable, good faith interpretation. The final regulations apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2027. A covered plan adopted in 2023 or later should already be defaulting new eligible employees into the plan.

Is the 3 percent default deferral an expense for the restaurant?

No. The deferral is withheld from the employee's pay and is a liability until it is deposited with the recordkeeper. Gross wages expense does not change. Only an employer match, if the plan provides one, is an employer expense.

Do part-time restaurant employees count toward the 10-employee exemption?

Yes. The final rule uses the COBRA counting method, under which part-time employees count as a fraction of a full-time employee based on hours worked. An employer normally employs more than 10 if it exceeded 10 on at least 50 percent of its typical business days in the preceding calendar year.

What if a restaurant's headcount falls back under 10 after a slow season?

The exemption does not return. Once an employer first exceeds 10 employees, the exemption ends after the one-year period following the close of that taxable year, and the automatic enrollment requirement continues for later plan years even if headcount drops below 10.
